reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Presents as a subacute, progressive pancerebellar syndrome with gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus, and often severe truncal instability over weeks to months
Frequently precedes the diagnosis of the causative tumour, so its recognition should prompt a systematic malignancy search
Anti-Yo (PCA-1) antibodies are strongly associated with gynaecological and breast cancers, typically in women
Anti-Hu and anti-Tr/DNER, anti-Ri, and anti-P/Q calcium-channel antibodies are linked with small-cell lung cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and other tumours
MRI is often normal early, later showing cerebellar atrophy, while antibody testing and tumour screening establish the diagnosis
The immune attack causes largely irreversible loss of Purkinje cells, so early treatment offers the best, though often limited, chance of stabilisation
Management combines treatment of the underlying tumour with immunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration arises when a systemic tumour expresses antigens also present in cerebellar neurons, most notably Purkinje cells. The immune response mounted against the tumour cross-reacts with these neuronal antigens, producing an immune-mediated attack on the cerebellum. Antibodies such as anti-Yo, anti-Hu, anti-Ri, and anti-Tr/DNER serve as diagnostic markers of specific antigen-tumour associations, while cytotoxic T-cell mechanisms are believed to drive the neuronal destruction in antibodies targeting intracellular antigens. Progressive, often irreversible loss of Purkinje cells underlies the clinical picture, explaining why cerebellar atrophy appears on later imaging and why neurological recovery is usually incomplete even when the tumour is treated.
additionalDifferentials: Immune-mediated cerebellar ataxia (e.g. anti-GAD, gluten ataxia)
Cerebellar metastasis or posterior fossa lesion
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid paraneoplastic/onconeural antibody panel (anti-Yo, anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Tr/DNER, anti-P/Q)
MRI brain to exclude structural lesions and assess for cerebellar atrophy
CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis and FDG-PET to identify an occult tumour
Mammography and pelvic/gynaecological imaging where anti-Yo is positive
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showing inflammatory changes or oligoclonal bands
Bloods including thiamine, vitamin, and metabolic screen to exclude mimics
redFlags: Rapidly progressive ataxia disabling gait within weeks
Positive onconeural antibodies indicating a high likelihood of underlying malignancy
Brainstem or bulbar involvement compromising swallow and airway
Accompanying encephalomyelitis or autonomic features suggesting a wider paraneoplastic process
reference.prognosis: Neurological outcome is generally poor because Purkinje cell loss is largely irreversible; treatment of the tumour and immunotherapy may halt progression but rarely restores function, and prognosis is heavily influenced by the underlying cancer.
pitfalls: Attributing subacute ataxia to alcohol or degeneration and missing an occult tumour
Stopping the malignancy search after initial imaging is negative rather than repeating surveillance
Delaying immunotherapy and tumour treatment while awaiting antibody results
Expecting full neurological recovery once the cancer is treated
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
